opening.headline: Find out why requests are delayed even when the GPU is idle through device allocation and scaling indicators, and determine the pros and cons of indicator-based scaling, event-based scaling, and scale-to-zero.
body: The utilization of the two GPU nodes is low, but the request queue continues to get longer, some pods do not receive GPUs and remain in the Pending state, and GPU costs continue to incur even though there are no requests at night. Although these three symptoms may seem different, they all stem from how GPU resources are matched to requests.

In this lesson, we first compare exposing the GPU as an extended resource with a device plugin and Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), which requests the device as a billing object. Next, we look at HPA's behavior and stabilization window, KEDA's event-based scaling, the fact that even if you increase the pod, the pod stays in Pending if there are no GPU nodes, how node-level scaling makes up for this, the costs and benefits of scale-to-zero, and the balance between load spikes and idle costs is explained with examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the roles of device plug-ins, DRA, HPA, and KEDA
You can distinguish between indicator-based scaling and event-based scaling.
The HPA's copy number calculation formula and metrics such as GPU utilization or queue length can explain the path to the HPA.
Explain the relationship between pod-level expansion and node-level expansion, and explain the flow of node expansion when a pod becomes pending.
You can judge the advantages and disadvantages of scale-to-zero

screens.title: GPU is idle but requests are delayed
screens.lead: Select each GPU node in the picture one by one to see why the GPU is empty. Even the same symptoms have different causes.

visual.alt: An illustration showing three GPU nodes and a request queue, with low GPU utilization on the nodes but a long queue.
labels: Unable to place due to label mismatch

items.prompt: Node A: Low utilization but long queue
items.answer: If requests aren't being processed at an acceptable rate and GPU utilization is low, the bottleneck may not be GPU computation. Requests may be concentrated in only one pod, CPU and network may be bottlenecks, or the metrics you based your scaling on may not reflect the actual bottleneck. In the LLM server, the step of generating tokens one by one does not use up the computational power of the GPU and tends to block memory access. Additionally, the intermediate calculation results (KV cache) accumulated for each request occupy GPU memory, so when the memory is full, new requests cannot be received simultaneously even if the calculation utilization is low. So the GPU utilization number alone doesn't tell us anything about queue build-up.

items.prompt: Node B: Pod is in Pending state and does not receive GPU
items.answer: If a Pod requests GPU resources and the scheduler does not find a suitable node, it remains Pending. This commonly occurs when the requested extension resource name is different from the name advertised by the node, or when no node has the required GPU type.

items.prompt: Node C: Not placed because label does not match
items.answer: Each node has a different GPU type, and if the pod does not write down the conditions for selecting the appropriate node, it will be placed on the wrong node or may not be deployed. It is necessary to match the node label and selection conditions.

items.prompt: Bam: There is no request, but only GPU costs are incurred.
items.answer: If you leave Minimal Replica always on, you will incur costs by having one or more GPUs reserved even when there is no request. The problem is dealing with peak load during the day and idle at night with the same settings.

screens.outro: Now that we have established that there are various causes, let us recall similar experiences.

screens.title: Think about it: between load and cost.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: The GPU is idle but requests are backlogged. Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: If GPU utilization is low but latencies are high, utilization is not an indicator of service health. We need to start by finding out what is actually being pushed out of that service.

items.prompt: Have you ever had an experience where the indicator you used as a basis for expansion was different from the actual bottleneck?
items.answer: CPU utilization was used as a criterion, but the bottleneck was often GPU memory or request queue. Matching the scaling metrics to the bottleneck is the starting point for autoscaling.

items.prompt: Are there expensive resources left on when no one is using them?
items.answer: GPUs cost a lot per hour, so idle time is wasted. Conversely, if you reduce it, there will be a delay when turning it back on. This balance is the final topic of this lesson.

screens.outro: First, let's look at how Kubernetes treats GPUs as a resource.

screens.title: Device plugins and GPU scheduling
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to see the GPU order from plugin to scheduler to pod.

visual.alt: Flow schematic where a node's GPU is advertised as an extension resource via a device plugin and the scheduler deploys pods.

steps.title: 1. Install drivers and plugins
steps.body: Administrators must install the GPU vendor's drivers on the node and run the vendor's device plug-ins. AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA all offer their own plugins.

steps.title: 2. Extension resources are exposed
steps.body: After installing the plug-in, your cluster exposes custom schedulable resources such as `amd.com/gpu` or `nvidia.com/gpu`. GPUs can be requested by resource name like CPU or memory.

steps.title: 3. Pod requests limits
steps.body: GPU is specified only in the `limits` entry. If you just write limits, Kubernetes uses the limits value as requests. When writing requests and limits together, the values ​​must be the same, and you cannot write only requests. For example, I request one copy like `gpu-vendor.example/example-gpu: 1`.

steps.title: 4. Scheduler places
steps.body: The scheduler selects nodes with the requested resources and places the pods on them. If each node has a different GPU type, the node label and selector are sent to the appropriate node, and Node Feature Discovery detects the hardware characteristics of the node and automatically labels it. Even conditions such as GPU memory can be expressed with node affinity.

screens.outro: Next, we will look at DRA, which was created to overcome the limitations of this method.

screens.title: Dynamic Resource Allocation: Request a device on your bill
screens.lead: Read the table and compare the differences between the device plug-in method and the DRA method, and the roles of the objects that make up DRA.

data.caption: Comparison of device plugins and DRA

data.notes: The benefit of DRA is that it classifies devices by type, providing app operators with hardware categories that are fit for purpose. However, DRA resources do not support preemption, so even high-priority pods may be Pending until their existing usage ends.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the device allocation, let's look at the HPA changing the number of replications depending on the load.

screens.title: HPA: Metric-Based Scaling
screens.lead: Use the slider to vary the length of the scale-down stabilization window and see how the number of copies varies under the same load.

visual.alt: Illustration comparing the request load curve and the copy number staircase graph as a function of stabilization window length.

stops.body: HPA watches metrics and adjusts the number of replications in a control loop with a default 15-second cycle. If the stabilization window is 0, reduce the number of replications as soon as the metric goes down. If the load fluctuates, flapping occurs where the number of replications continues to fluctuate, and you have to increase it again right after reducing it, resulting in repeated model loading costs.

Decrease based on the highest value calculated over the last 60 seconds. Short bursts are filtered out, but the replication count is maintained for a minute or so even when the load actually decreases.

A common setting for reducing is a 5-minute window. The rate of rise and fall is controlled by the `scaleUp` and `scaleDown` policies of `behavior`, and the stabilization window prevents the copy number from fluctuating. For services with high startup costs, such as model servers, it is appropriate to have a long window on the decreasing side and a short window on the expanding side.

stops.value: Copy number calculation formula and tolerances
stops.body: HPA calculates the number of replications required as the ratio of the metric's current value to its target value. The expression is `desiredReplicas = ceil[currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue]`. For example, if the average metric for 4 pods is twice your target, calculate that you need 8; if it's half your target, reduce it to 2. If the ratio of the current value to the target value is close enough to 1, no adjustment is made; this tolerance defaults to 0.1 (10%). This tolerance ensures that the number of replications does not change even if the indicator vacillates slightly near the target.

Pod-specific resource metrics, such as CPU, are calculated as utilization compared to requests, averaged across all target pods, and the number of replications is calculated as the ratio of the average to the target. So if you have a container without requests, the utilization is undefined and HPA will not do anything with that metric. Also, in GPU services, CPU utilization may not reflect the actual bottleneck, so indicators such as queue length or number of requests must be considered.

HPA queries metrics from the control plane's aggregate API. Resource metrics are metrics.k8s.io, custom metrics are custom.metrics.k8s.io, and external metrics outside the cluster are external.metrics.k8s.io. The Resource Metrics API is usually provided by an add-on called Metrics Server and must be installed separately. Custom metrics and external metrics require an adapter API server provided by your metrics solution to be read. Therefore, scaling with either GPU utilization or queue length requires two steps. First, a collector must gather the metrics (for example, DCGM-Exporter exports GPU metrics in Prometheus format), and then an adapter must expose the metrics to its metrics API. If any of these paths are missing, HPA will not be able to read the metrics and will not expand.

screens.outro: Let's compare it to KEDA, which looks at events instead of indicators.

ext.title: Kubernetes Docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Algorithm details, Support for metrics APIs)

screens.title: KEDA and event-based scaling
screens.lead: Alternate between the two states and compare how the timing of response and the components involved change in the same cue backlog situation.

states.label: Indicator-based (HPA)
states.body: HPA periodically queries metrics to calculate the number of replications. There must be at least one pod running for metrics to be collected, and if the metric is tied to the pod's resource usage, such as utilization relative to requests, it will not respond as work piles up in the queue unless utilization increases. Resource metrics such as CPU or memory are measured only in running pods, so they cannot lead to scaling that restarts with 0 pods. HPAs that use external metrics, such as queue length, can set minReplicas to 0, but they must have a separate adapter to supply those metrics to the HPA.

states.label: Event-based (KEDA)
states.body: KEDA monitors event sources such as queues, topics, and databases to provide metrics to HPA and drive scaling. Declare `pollingInterval` (default 30 seconds), `cooldownPeriod` (default 300 seconds), `minReplicaCount`, `maxReplicaCount` in ScaledObject with target and trigger. Decrease to 0 if there are no messages waiting, and activate when a message arrives. Activation from 0 to 1 is handled by KEDA, and expansion from 1 to N is handled by HPA. If `minReplicaCount` is greater than 0, it will not be decremented to 0 and the HPA will be responsible for scaling.

screens.outro: Let's look at the pros and cons of reducing to 0 when there are no events.

screens.title: Pod Scaling and Node Scaling: Two Layers of Autoscaling
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to increase the number of replications by HPA or KEDA, then follow the flow until the pod becomes Pending and nodes are added to receive requests.

visual.alt: A two-tiered schematic where pod-level scaling increases replication, and node autoscalers add GPU nodes when empty pods become Pending.

steps.title: 1. Pod layer increases replication count
steps.body: As requests increase, HPA or KEDA increases the number of replications in the Deployment to create more pods. This layer only determines the number of pods. I don't know where the GPUs that can run those pods are located.

steps.title: 2. If there are no seats, it becomes pending.
steps.body: A new pod requests GPU limits, but if the existing node's GPUs are all used up, the scheduler cannot find a node to place on, and the pod stays in Pending. The number of replications has increased, but the number of pods receiving requests has not increased. A configuration that only increases pods without nodes will not solve the queuing problem.

steps.title: 3. Node autoscaler adds nodes
steps.body: The node autoscaler sees pods that cannot be placed on existing nodes, creates a node that can accommodate those pods using the cloud provider's API, and adds them to the cluster. This is called provisioning, and the Kubernetes documentation introduces Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter as representative implementations. The inputs for the decision are the pod's scheduling constraints (resource requests, node affinity, etc.) and the node configuration set in the autoscaler.

steps.title: 4. Nodes are ready and pods receive requests
steps.body: When a new node joins the cluster, GPU drivers and device plugins are prepared, and then Pending pods are deployed. After receiving the image, loading the model, and passing readiness, the request is received. Therefore, the response time to a spike in load is the sum of node creation time, image transmission time, and model loading time. If response time is an issue, choose to have spare GPU nodes upfront or increase minimum replication.

steps.title: 5. When reducing, it is organized in the opposite direction.
steps.body: As load decreases and the HPA reduces replication, some nodes become empty or underused. Node autoscalers reduce costs by organizing these nodes, which is called consolidation. Provisioning and integration are both based on requests, not actual usage of the pods. So, if the requests are incorrect, the node is calculated as either under or over.

steps.title: 6. Set the two floors together
steps.body: If there is only a pod layer, Pending accumulates when GPUs are insufficient, and if there is only a node layer, replication does not increase, so it is judged that there is no need for new nodes. A common configuration is a combination of metric-based pod scaling and node scaling, where the balance between first request delay and GPU cost is key to the design.

screens.outro: Now that we've connected the two layers, let's look at the pros and cons of choosing to reduce to zero.

screens.title: scale-to-zero and inference pool
screens.lead: Select each tab to explore the benefits and costs of scale-to-zero and the concept of inference pools.

tabs.label: advantage
tabs.body: scale-to-zero eliminates idle costs by reducing pods to zero while there are no requests. For high-cost resources such as GPUs, the cost of long periods of time with little load, such as nights and weekends, is greatly eliminated.

tabs.label: price
tabs.body: When the first request comes, there is a delay as it has to wait while the pods are started and the model is loaded. If the GPU node is reduced to 0, the delay will be longer due to the addition of the time to create a new node and the time to receive the image. The larger the model, the longer the delay, making it unsuitable for services that cannot tolerate user waiting. Receiving traffic or hitting a health check before the model has finished loading can lead to a request failure, so you need to guard against this delay by setting up probes to determine readiness.

tabs.label: cooldownPeriod
tabs.body: `cooldownPeriod` determines how long to wait after the last event before decrementing to 0. The default is 300 seconds. If it is too short, it will drop to 0 even in short intervals, causing frequent first request delays; if it is too long, it will leave idle costs behind.

tabs.label: inference pool
tabs.body: An inference pool is a collection of pods that serve the same model in the same way. Scaling is a matter of changing the number of copies of this bundle, and which pod will receive the request is a separate routing issue. You can configure it to match latency needs with the smallest replica always on, and scale the load above that with a queue metric. Whether to keep the minimum of one or reduce it to zero depends on your delay requirements.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to the example and start by reading about how a device claim is attached to a pod.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Read how DRA resource claims are attached to pods
screens.lead: This is a situation where a pod needs one GPU with certain properties. Select the right arrow to follow the YAML as the claim is linked to the pod.

steps.title: Step 1: Find out what device you have
steps.body: The device owner's driver publishes the node's device information as a ResourceSlice. Before creating a claim, determine what properties devices exist in your cluster. With this information, you can determine whether the terms of your claim are realistic.

steps.title: Step 2: Create a Claim Template
steps.body:
The workload operator creates a ResourceClaimTemplate that references the DeviceClass.

```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata:
  name: example-resource-claim-template
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: gpu-claim
        exactly:
          deviceClassName: example-device-class
          selectors:
            - cel:
                expression: |-
                  device.attributes["driver.example.com"].type == "gpu" &&
                  device.capacity["driver.example.com"].memory == quantity("64Gi")
```

Filter device type and memory capacity with CEL expression.

steps.title: Step 3: Pod references claim
steps.body: You reference the claim by name in `resourceClaims` in the pod spec, and associate the usage by that name in `resources.claims` in the container. If you use `resourceClaimTemplateName`, a separate claim is created for each pod, and if you use `resourceClaimName`, multiple containers or pods share an already existing claim. In the Job example in the documentation, one container uses an independent claim and two containers use a shared claim.

steps.title: Step 4: Scheduler and Driver Finalize
steps.body: The scheduler places pods on nodes that satisfy the claim, and the driver attaches the device to a container. If no device meets the conditions, the pod remains Pending. Even if there is a device that meets the conditions, if another pod is using it, DRA resources cannot be preempted, so it waits until they are finished using them.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: If you only write down the quantity in the device plugin, in DRA you write down what you want as an attribute. The trade-off is that the number of objects increases, so check first that your billing template and class name are correct.

screens.outro: Next, we will solve the expansion policy equilibrium as an example.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Balance between load spikes and idle costs
screens.lead: There is a surge in requests during the day and virtually no service at night. Select the arrows to the right to compare the costs and delays of the three policies.

steps.title: sorting out the situation
steps.body: During the day, there are a lot of requests, requiring a large increase in the number of replications, while at night there are very few requests. Assume that the cost of one GPU is large and model loading takes time. We compare the three policies in terms of cost, first request delay, and operational complexity.

steps.title: Policy A: Use only HPA and maintain a minimum replication of 1
steps.body: Depending on the load, HPA adjusts the number of copies, keeping the minimum number of copies at 1. The first request in the morning is received by a pod that is already floating, so the response is fast. Instead, one GPU is left on at night, leaving idle costs.

steps.title: Policy B: Watch queue length with KEDA and scale down to 0
steps.body: If you use queue length as trigger and leave minReplicaCount as 0, all pods will disappear at night. Idle costs are minimal, but the first request in the morning has to wait for pod startup and model loading. Only suitable for services where first request delay is acceptable.

steps.title: Policy C: Minimum timephased replication and long stabilization window
steps.body: Increase minimum replication during the day, lower it at night, and leave a longer scaleDown stabilization window. It reduces delay by preparing in advance just before a surge, and prevents flapping by not immediately reducing replication even when the load is briefly turned off. This is a good compromise when load patterns are predictable.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Set policies with delay tolerance and load predictability. If delay is not acceptable, A or C is suitable. If delay is acceptable and the load is intermittent, B is suitable. For any policy, we must first check whether the scaling metric is the same as the actual bottleneck.

screens.outro: Let me summarize the key points by combining the two cases.

screens.title: TL;DR: Choosing device allocation and scaling
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: Device plugins expose devices such as GPUs as extended resources, and DRA requests devices as claim objects. In clusters with mixed GPU types, placement is controlled using labels and Node Feature Discovery.

HPA controls the number of replications by looking at metrics, and KEDA monitors event sources to drive expansion. Activation from 0 to 1 is handled by KEDA, and expansion from 1 to N is handled by HPA. The HPA behavior policy and stabilization window refine the rise and fall rate to prevent flapping.

Pod-level scaling and node-level scaling are different layers. Even if HPA or KEDA increases replication, if there are no GPU nodes, the pod becomes Pending, and the node autoscaler sees this and adds a node. The first request delay includes node creation, image transfer, and model loading times. The HPA's replication count is calculated as the ratio of the current metric and the target metric, and GPU utilization or queue length must pass through the collector and adapter to reach the HPA.

Scale-to-zero trades idle cost savings for first request delay. Delays are tolerated and the load is only suitable for intermittent services, otherwise it maintains minimal replication or throttling by time of day.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Autoscaling starts with matching metrics to bottlenecks. Even the most sophisticated policies are useless if the indicators do not reflect the actual bottlenecks.

glossary.def: This is a method of notifying Kubernetes of a device such as a node's GPU as an extended resource.
A device allocation method that claims devices with ResourceClaim and supports sharing and attribute filters.

A controller that calculates the number of replications as a ratio of the current metric and the target metric. The rising and falling speed is controlled by the behavior's scaleUp and scaleDown policies and the stabilization window.
A custom resource in KEDA that declares the scale target and trigger, polling cycle, cooldown, and copy number range.
This method eliminates idle costs by reducing the number of pods to 0 when there are no requests.
This is a component that sees pods that cannot be scheduled, adds nodes, and cleans up less used nodes. Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter are representative examples.

misconceptions.myth: GPU services also scale well with CPU utilization.
misconceptions.fact: The bottleneck may be the request queue or GPU memory, so CPU utilization may not reflect the load. Scaling metric selection is important.
KEDA monitors event sources and supplies indicators to the HPA, taking on activations between 0 and 1. Extensions beyond 1 are handled by HPA.
Idle costs are reduced, but the first request will have to wait for pod startup and model loading. This is only true for services where first request delays are acceptable.

misconceptions.myth: As long as you set HPA or KEDA, even if the GPU is insufficient, it will be resolved automatically.
misconceptions.fact: HPA and KEDA only change the number of pods. If no nodes have GPUs, new pods will remain Pending and will not be deployed until the node autoscaler adds nodes.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Device plugins expose devices and DRA claims devices.
HPA expands to indicators, KEDA expands to events, and behavior prevents fluctuations.
scale-to-zero trades idle cost for first request delay.
Pod scaling and node scaling are different layers, and the first request delay also includes node creation time.
